DkMwYxfSYNQ.title: The Why, What, and How of Pinning in Rust
DkMwYxfSYNQ.summary: Jon Gjengset's long live-coding stream explains Rust's Pin and Unpin types: why they exist, how they work, and how they connect to futures and async/await. It also covers moving from pre-pinning code to the new model.
DkMwYxfSYNQ.why_hn: HN treats it as the definitive resource for understanding Pin semantics and lists it among async Rust learning materials.

categories.name: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages

quote.text: Jon Gjengset's stream on pin/unpin is invaluable for understanding Pin semantics

RzWB5jL5RX0.title: Cracking Enigma in 2021 - Computerphile
RzWB5jL5RX0.summary: Dr Mike Pound of Computerphile shows how a modern laptop can crack Enigma, using a ciphertext-only attack based on an older paper. He compares it with the tooling in CrypTool.
RzWB5jL5RX0.why_hn: HN recommends it as a good starting point on practical Enigma cryptanalysis with modern hardware.

quote.text: would be a good place to start.

VkIJbpdTujE.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting! - Computerphile
VkIJbpdTujE.summary: A Computerphile video in which Dr Mike Pound and PhD student Lewis Stuart explain 3D Gaussian splatting, a quick technique that turns photos of a scene into a 3D model without much compute. It includes a demo and compares the approach to NeRFs.
VkIJbpdTujE.why_hn: HN recommends it as an accessible introduction to Gaussian splats, made by people who understand the subject.

quote.text: Here's a much better explainer from some people who seem to actually understand the subject matter and not just the buzzwords

rAl-9HwD858.title: Crust of Rust: Lifetime Annotations
rAl-9HwD858.summary: In this first Crust of Rust episode, Jon Gjengset live-codes an example that needs multiple explicit lifetime annotations. Along the way he covers string types and generics over a custom trait.
rAl-9HwD858.why_hn: Recommended as a slow-paced, detailed live-coding session that makes lifetimes click once you are past Rust basics.

categories.name: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages

quote.text: each one is actually writing carefully chosen code that runs and talking through what's going on

rURRYI66E54.title: AI Language Models & Transformers - Computerphile
rURRYI66E54.summary: Rob Miles explains on Computerphile how language models generate plausible text and how transformers improved on recurrent networks, with a look at what comes next.
rURRYI66E54.why_hn: Pointed to as an accessible early explanation of transformers and attention for newcomers.

quote.text: You can check-out his other videos on NLP as well they are all excellent.

EL7Au1tzNxE.title: Vibe coding complex changes in Rust
EL7Au1tzNxE.summary: Jon Gjengset spends about three hours livecoding complex changes in a Rust codebase with agentic AI tools, testing his hypothesis that AI is weak at non-pattern work. He documents where Claude Code helps and where it struggles.
EL7Au1tzNxE.why_hn: Pointed to as a non-promotional, realistic long session of an experienced engineer working with AI on non-trivial code.

categories.name: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages

quote.text: I found this one and sat down and watched the whole three hours.

ThjvMReOXYM.title: Crust of Rust: async/await
ThjvMReOXYM.summary: Jon Gjengset's long live-coding Crust of Rust episode on async/await, focused on the mental model for using it rather than on Futures, Pin and Wakers internals. Topics include awaiting multiple futures, cancellation, executors and select.
ThjvMReOXYM.why_hn: Recommended as a deep, practical dive for learning how Rust async works.

categories.name: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages

quote.text: these two videos are also great deep dives into Rust async

WO2X3oZEJOA.title: Glitch Tokens - Computerphile
WO2X3oZEJOA.summary: Rob Miles explains "glitch" tokens, odd strings in large language model vocabularies that make the model produce gibberish. He covers how they likely arise from tokenizer training data, such as Reddit usernames, that never appeared in the model's own training.
WO2X3oZEJOA.why_hn: HN points to it as the accessible explanation of why glitch tokens exist whenever tokenizers or odd GPT behavior come up.

quote.text: it's also a good introduction to the topic.

jf_ddGnum_4.title: Implementing (part of) a BitTorrent client in Rust
jf_ddGnum_4.summary: Jon Gjengset's roughly four-hour live stream implementing part of a BitTorrent client in Rust, following CodeCrafters' test-guided challenge. He builds from scratch and shows idiomatic error handling along the way.
jf_ddGnum_4.why_hn: HN recommends it as a comprehensive walkthrough of the build-your-own-BitTorrent challenge and as an introduction to CodeCrafters.

categories.name: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages

quote.text: Jon Gjengset did a comprehensive stream going through the Build your own BitTorrent challenge

s19G6n0UjsM.title: Rust at speed — building a fast concurrent database
s19G6n0UjsM.summary: A guest lecture Jon Gjengset gave at Two Sigma on using Rust for large, high-performance systems. It covers why Rust suits such projects, the Noria research database, a concurrent data structure used in it, and practical experience.
s19G6n0UjsM.why_hn: HN points to it as a detailed, captivating talk by the Noria author, including a good explanation of deduplicating data between maps using unsafe.

categories.name: C, C++, Rust, Go & systems languages

quote.text: gave a great talk about the system

viJt_DXTfwA.title: ChatGPT with Rob Miles - Computerphile
viJt_DXTfwA.summary: Computerphile interviews AI safety researcher Rob Miles about ChatGPT: how it was trained with human feedback, why it tends to produce confident nonsense, and where it may or may not be dangerous.
viJt_DXTfwA.why_hn: HN commenters send it to people confused about ChatGPT's quirks, explaining how human-feedback training makes it a pleasing yes-man that bullshits.

quote.text: This video[1] cleared up a lot of questions for me as to the issues I've seen with ChatGPT.

NTfOnGZUZDk.title: Where GREP Came From - Computerphile
NTfOnGZUZDk.summary: Brian Kernighan explains how grep came to be, written overnight by Ken Thompson, and how it got its name from the ed command g/re/p. He also covers the lineage from QED to ed that led to it.
NTfOnGZUZDk.why_hn: HN commenters point to it as a short, charming first-hand account of Unix history from someone who was there.

quote.text: My favourite BWK video is about grep.

GctxvSPIfr8.title: Thesis: Partial State in Dataflow-Based Materialized Views
GctxvSPIfr8.summary: Jon Gjengset's 2020 PhD dissertation presentation at MIT on partial state in dataflow-based materialized views, the idea behind the Noria database. The Q&A is cut out.
GctxvSPIfr8.why_hn: HN points to it, including Gjengset himself, as a more digestible way into partially-stateful dataflow than the thesis text, mostly in caching and database threads.

XZJc1p6RE78.title: Ch(e)at GPT? - Computerphile
XZJc1p6RE78.summary: Computerphile video in which Mike Pound explains a University of Maryland paper on watermarking LLM output. The method biases token choices so generated text can later be detected statistically.
XZJc1p6RE78.why_hn: Linked as the approachable explanation whenever HN discusses detecting or watermarking AI-generated text.

quote.text: a nice very approachable video explaining it here

nybVFJVXbww.title: Elliptic Curve Back Door - Computerphile
nybVFJVXbww.summary: Dr Mike Pound explains the suspected backdoor in the Dual_EC_DRBG random number generator and how elliptic curve constants could let someone predict its output.
nybVFJVXbww.why_hn: HN points to it as an intuitive explanation of how NIST standardized a backdoored generator.

quote.text: He also gives a super cool/intuitive breakdown on how this came to be.

_8yVOC4ciXc.title: GPT3: An Even Bigger Language Model - Computerphile
_8yVOC4ciXc.summary: Rob Miles discusses GPT-3 on Computerphile, covering how scaling parameters kept improving results over GPT-2 and how the model nearly learned arithmetic without anyone knowing exactly how.
_8yVOC4ciXc.why_hn: HN commenters cite it as a concise explanation of GPT-3's scaling jump and surprising abilities at its release.

quote.text: Computerphile summed it up pretty well on GPT-3's release
